Field surveys of Cleftbelly trevally (Atropus atropos) in the coastal waters of the eastern Indian Ocean have provided robust estimates of several key life-history parameters. The asymptotic total length, representing the maximum size an individual can attain under typical environmental conditions, was determined to be 31.6 cm [Li = 31.6 cm], a value consistent with the moderate body size characteristic of this carangid species. In contrast, the total length at which 50% of individuals exhibit signs of gonadal maturation, marking the onset of puberty, was recorded at 17.1 cm [Lp = 17.1 cm]. This substantial size difference between maturation and ultimate length suggests a prolonged adult growth phase, which is common among iteroparous tropical teleosts that continue somatic expansion well after reproductive activity has commenced. These length-based metrics were derived from a large sample of individuals collected across multiple seasons, providing a reliable basis for understanding the species' size structure and demographic patterns.

Reproductive investment in Cleftbelly trevally is substantial, as evidenced by fecundity estimates obtained from gravid females captured during the peak of the spawning season. At a body size of 25.3 cm total length, a single female can produce up to 372,344 oocytes per spawning event [N_R_i = up to 372,344 oocytes per spawning event], a remarkably high fecundity that aligns with the species' broadcast-spawning strategy in a productive tropical environment. Females typically complete two distinct spawning events within a single season [F_R_i = two distinct spawning events within a single season], maximizing their annual reproductive output. This entire reproductive process unfolds under the warm thermal conditions characteristic of the region, with a sustained water temperature of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C] providing the metabolic foundation for oocyte development and high-frequency spawning. The combination of large clutch size and repeated spawning likely buffers against the high mortality faced by pelagic eggs and larvae.

The early life stages of Cleftbelly trevally begin with remarkably small offspring, a pattern typical of pelagic-spawning carangids that produce large numbers of minute propagules. The wet weight at birth, corresponding to the moment of eclosion from the yolk-dependent egg, is approximately 0.0000477 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0000477 grams], reflecting an initial body size that is among the smallest recorded for this genus. This minuscule mass is a direct consequence of the species' egg diameter of 0.45 millimeters, which yields a minimal per-offspring investment but enables the production of hundreds of thousands of eggs over a single spawning season. Under the ambient thermal regime of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C], the period from fertilisation to egg hatching is compressed, with the yolk-sac larva emerging after just 4 days [ab = 4 days]. This rapid embryonic development is an adaptive response to warm tropical waters, where elevated temperatures accelerate metabolic processes and reduce the window of vulnerability during the early, defenseless pelagic phase.

Growth trajectories reconstructed from otolith increment analysis and length-frequency data reveal the substantial mass changes that accompany the species' progression through juvenile and adult life stages. Upon reaching the size at which pubertal development is initiated, individuals typically achieve a wet weight of 72.2 grams [Wwp = 72.2 grams], a mass that corresponds closely to the 17.1 cm length threshold for gonadal activation. This represents only a modest fraction of the ultimate adult body mass, which peaks at 420.8 grams [Wwi = 420.8 grams] for fully grown, asymptotic individuals of the maximum total length. The more than five-fold increase from pubertal to asymptotic wet weight underscores a life-history strategy that prioritises continued somatic growth well beyond the onset of reproductive maturity, a pattern that is energetically feasible in the productive tropical ecosystems where this species resides. These mass-based estimates were derived from species-specific length-weight regressions validated against field-collected specimens.

Longevity estimates for Cleftbelly trevally indicate a moderate lifespan relative to other carangids of similar body size, with the maximum recorded lifespan in the wild reaching approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] when maintained under the prevailing thermal conditions of 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C]. This relatively short generation time, combined with early maturation at around 17.1 cm total length, suggests a life-history strategy that balances moderate adult survival against high fecundity and rapid juvenile growth. The species' age at birth, marking the transition from the incubating egg to the free-swimming larval phase, occurs after a brief 4-day incubation period (4 days) [ab = 4 days] at 28.2 °C [T = 28.2 °C], a rapid developmental timeline that is characteristic of tropical pelagic spawners. Field observations confirm that the vast majority of natural mortality occurs during the early pelagic larval and juvenile stages, with survivors reaching reproductive ages within their first year.
